entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen22300" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> The psalmist encourages himself to praise the Lord for mercies he had received, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.1-Psa.108.5">Psa 108:1-5</reference>. He prays for the Divine succor, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.6">Psa 108:6</reference>; and encourages the people to expect their restoration, and the enjoyment of all their former privileges and possessions, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.7-Psa.108.13">Psa 108:7-13</reference>. <div eID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is compounded of two Psalms which we have had already under review. The <reference osisRef="Psa.108.1">Psa 108:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.2">Psa 108:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.3">Psa 108:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.4">Psa 108:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.108.5">Psa 108:5</reference>, are the same with the <reference osisRef="Psa.57.7">Psa 57:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.8">Psa 57:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.9">Psa 57:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.10">Psa 57:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.57.11">Psa 57:11</reference> of <reference osisRef="Psa.57.1-Psa.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference> : And the <reference osisRef="Psa.108.6">Psa 108:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.7">Psa 108:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.8">Psa 108:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.9">Psa 108:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.10">Psa 108:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.11">Psa 108:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.12">Psa 108:12</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.108.13">Psa 108:13</reference>, are the same with the <reference osisRef="Psa.60.5">Psa 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.6">Psa 60:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.7">Psa 60:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.8">Psa 60:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.10">Psa 60:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.11">Psa 60:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.60.12">Psa 60:12</reference> of <reference osisRef="Psa.60.1-Psa.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference> : The variations are few, and of little moment, and the explanation may be seen in the notes on the preceding Psalms, which need not be repeated here. That the Pssalms referred to were made by David, and were applicable to the then state of his affairs, has been the opinion of many; and it is probable that the captives in Babylon composed this out of two above, and applied it to the state of their affairs. Their captivity being now ended, or nearly at an end they look and pray for their restoration to their own land, as amply as it was possessed in the most prosperous days of David. The Syriac considers it as a prophecy of the vocation of the Gentiles. The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute it to David. <div eID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> Even with my glory - My greatest glory shall be in publishing thy praise. Some make the glory here to mean the Lord himself; some, the Ark of the covenant; some, the Soul of the psalmist; others, his Tongue; some, the Gift of Prophecy; and some, the psalmist's Spirit or Vein of poetry. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.57.8">Psa 57:8</reference>.
entries.content_plain: Introduction The psalmist encourages himself to praise the Lord for mercies he had received, Psa 108:1-5 . He prays for the Divine succor, Psa 108:6 ; and encourages the people to expect their restoration, and the enjoyment of all their former privileges and possessions, Psa 108:7-13 . This Psalm is compounded of two Psalms which we have had already under review. The Psa 108:1 , Psa 108:2 , Psa 108:3 , Psa 108:4 , and Psa 108:5 , are the same with the Psa 57:7 , Psa 57:8 , Psa 57:9 , Psa 57:10 , and Psa 57:11 of Psa 57:1-11 : And the Psa 108:6 , Psa 108:7 , Psa 108:8 , Psa 108:9 , Psa 108:10 , Psa 108:11 , Psa 108:12 , and Psa 108:13 , are the same with the Psa 60:5 , Psa 60:6 , Psa 60:7 , Psa 60:8 , Psa 60:9 , Psa 60:10 , Psa 60:11 , and Psa 60:12 of Psa 60:1-12 : The variations are few, and of little moment, and the explanation may be seen in the notes on the preceding Psalms, which need not be repeated here. That the Pssalms referred to were made by David, and were applicable to the then state of his affairs, has been the opinion of many; and it is probable that the captives in Babylon composed this out of two above, and applied it to the state of their affairs. Their captivity being now ended, or nearly at an end they look and pray for their restoration to their own land, as amply as it was possessed in the most prosperous days of David. The Syriac considers it as a prophecy of the vocation of the Gentiles. The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute it to David. Verse 1 Even with my glory - My greatest glory shall be in publishing thy praise. Some make the glory here to mean the Lord himself; some, the Ark of the covenant; some, the Soul of the psalmist; others, his Tongue; some, the Gift of Prophecy; and some, the psalmist's Spirit or Vein of poetry. See the notes on Psa 57:8 .

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> Among the people - The Jews. <div eID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22308" type="x-p"/> Among the nations - The Gentiles. Wherever this Psalm is sung or read, either among Jews or Gentiles, David may be said to sing praise to God.
